title: A Cat's Meow
full_review:
Glamour, power, intrigue and jealousy collide aboard William Randolf Hearst's extravagant yacht during the airy retelling of an infamous 1924 weekend in "The Cat's Meow" (Lions Gate).

In piecing together the gossip and whispers surrounding the death of film pioneer Thomas Ince, director Peter Bogdanovich has fashioned an intriguing narrative about what supposedly happened that fateful weekend. Commenting on the power of status and wealth in Tinseltown, Bogdanovich doesn't lose sight of the entertainment value of this Hollywood saga. Famed publisher W.R. Hearst (Edward Herrmann) gathered several of his more colorful friends, including his much younger mistress, actress Marion Davies (a wonderful Kirsten Dunst), for a romping weekend aboard the Oneida to celebrate the birthday of Ince (Cary Elwes). But the fun ended when the yacht docked abruptly and Ince's limp body was carried off. A few days later, Ince was dead. The cause of his death was never truly known.

With its opulent costume and set designs, well-crafted script and Hollywood scandal material, "The Cat's Meow" is an engaging drama supported by solid ensemble performances. The audience meets the characters as they board the boat, excited to partake in the generosity of their host, W.R. Framed by black-and-white flashbacks of Ince's funeral, the film is more of a mild whodunit (especially for a younger adult audience unfamiliar with the personalities and circumstances) than an out-and-out thriller. It is the secrets, rumors and innuendos of the sailing party that keep the viewer interested. And even in the last quarter when the film takes on a more grave tone, the focus of the film is on the machinations of the cover-up rather than the fact that a murder might have been committed.

The guests include the brilliant but self-absorbed Charlie Chaplin (Eddie Izzard), producer Ince preoccupied with his recent financial setbacks, ambitious gossip columnist -- and employee of W.R. -- Louella Parsons (Jennifer Tilly), and the eccentric British Victorian novelist Elinor Glyn (Joanna Lumley, dripping with British sophistication), who in voice-over narration explains to the viewer that although this may not be the whole story, it is the "whisper told most often."

As the festivities get under way, everyone has a secret agenda. Ince, realizing he's losing his earlier clout as an industry pioneer, is determined to merge his operations with W.R.'s more lucrative Cosmopolitan Pictures, despite W.R.'s seeming lack of interest. Awkward and star-struck Louella, based in New York, has set her sights on a transfer to Los Angeles, where she can cover the film industry more intimately. Ince's lover, actress Margaret Livingston (Claudia Harrison) no longer cares to keep their affair a secret. W.R. suspects that his young paramour Davies has been unfaithful to him with the legendary comic Chaplin. And Chaplin indeed schemes to lure away the beautiful actress from the richest man on earth.

A setup like this could have easily gotten muddled or overbearing. Yet Bogdanovich keeps the action moving along smoothly, feeding the audience narrative information while allowing the film to be a visual potpourri of glitz, charm and lavish luxury. Though a few biting remarks about Hollywood and its excess, class and wealth are slipped in, the film is not a serious indictment of rampant corruption. In a pointedly amusing scene, Louella and Margaret attempt to play ping-pong. As the balls constantly volley off the table, it is the attending servants that madly chase them around the floor while the ladies wait for the balls to be retrieved to resume their game.

His first theatrical feature after nine years, Bogdanovich may disappoint his fans by having uncharacteristically chosen much lighter fare this time around. But "The Cat's Meow" has charm and presence even if it's mostly played as sporty fun.

Due to a sexual encounter, some violence, fleeting nudity, brief drug use and sporadic profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
